title: Godel machine
summary:
The Godel machine is a hypothetical self-improving artificial intelligence invented by Jurgen Schmidhuber in 2003. It is a universal problem solver encoded as a completely self-referential program capable of rewriting any part of itself, provided it can prove that the rewrite is useful according to some utility function encoded within itself.

The Godel machine consists of two main parts. The solver interacts with some environment and determines utility using a reward function embedded in the machine. The searcher seeks to improve the entire Godel machine in a provably optimal way, subject to Godel's limits of provability.

The Godel machine relies on several types of axioms. Hardware axioms formally specify how components of the machine could change from one cycle to the next. Reward axioms define the computational cost of hardware instruction and the physical cost of output actions. Environment axioms restrict the way new inputs are produced from the environment. Uncertainty and string manipulation axioms are standard axioms for arithmetic, calculus, probability theory, and string manipulation. Utility axioms describe the overall goal in the form of a utility function.

According to Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem, any formal system that encompasses arithmetic is either flawed or allows for statements that cannot be proved in the system. Hence even a Godel machine with unlimited computational resources must ignore those self-improvements whose effectiveness it cannot prove. Schmidhuber points out that the Godel machine could start out by implementing AIXItl as its initial sub-program and self-modify after it finds proof that another algorithm will be better. The Darwin Godel Machine, a more recent development, abandoned rigorous mathematical proof in favor of empirical validation through evolutionary approaches.
